name: Shader basics & recipes
about: The foundations of shaders in Unity, whatever tool you use: what a shader is, how vertex and fragment stages work, UVs, normals, depth and custom functions, plus small self-contained recipes. Start here before moving to a specific effect. Use the "Built with" filter to see only Shader Graph or only HLSL guides.

name: Lighting & shadows
about: Lighting decides how a scene feels, and it spans real-time lights, baked lightmaps, light probes, reflection probes and shadows. These guides explain how each one works, how to tune quality against cost, and how to get a specific mood. Useful when your scene looks flat or when your frame time is going into shadows.

name: Post-processing & image effects
about: Post-processing runs on the finished image: bloom, colour grading, depth of field, vignettes, custom full-screen effects. Here you will find the Volume system in URP and HDRP, plus how to write your own full-screen passes. It is the quickest way to change the overall look of a game.

name: Render pipelines & SRP
about: The render pipeline controls how Unity turns a scene into pixels. These guides cover URP and HDRP choices, the Scriptable Render Pipeline, renderer features, custom passes and Render Graph. Read this section if you are choosing a pipeline, migrating, or extending rendering in a way the defaults do not allow.

name: Compute shaders & GPU
about: Compute shaders let the GPU do general-purpose work: simulations, particles, culling, procedural meshes and image processing. These guides cover dispatching compute work, buffers, GPU instancing and indirect drawing. Worth learning once your CPU is the bottleneck for work that can run in parallel.

name: Volumetrics & fog
about: Fog, light shafts, clouds and atmospheric scattering add depth that flat lighting cannot. This section covers raymarched volumes, height fog, god rays and volumetric lighting in Unity. These effects are costly, so many guides also show how to fake them cheaply.

name: Glass, refraction & transparency
about: Glass, water surfaces, ice and anything see-through are harder than they look: sorting, refraction, depth and reflections all interact. These guides cover blending modes, refraction using the scene colour, frosted and stained glass, and the fixes for common sorting artefacts.

name: Vertex displacement & animation
about: Moving vertices in the shader lets you animate meshes for free on the GPU: waving grass, flags, wobbling jelly, melting and morphing. This section explains displacement, vertex colours as animation masks and how to keep normals and shadows correct after the mesh has moved.

name: UVs, triplanar & texturing
about: How textures map onto surfaces is the foundation of most materials. These guides cover UV tricks, triplanar mapping for objects without good UVs, tiling, texture blending and scrolling. A good place to look if textures stretch, seam or repeat visibly.

name: Stencil, masks & decals
about: The stencil buffer and masking techniques let you cut holes, reveal hidden worlds, draw portals and project decals. This section covers stencil tests in shaders, render objects features in URP, and decal approaches. It is a small topic with a lot of clever effects.

name: Toon & cel shading
about: Cel and toon shading give a hand-drawn, anime or comic look through stepped lighting, rim light and flat colours. These guides cover ramp textures, custom lighting functions and stylised shadows, and how to match the looks of well-known games.

name: Outlines & edge detection
about: Outlines make characters and objects readable and stylised. Techniques here include inverted hulls, edge detection on depth and normals, and Fresnel-based rims. The guides compare cost, quality and compatibility so you can pick the right one for your pipeline.

name: Pixel art, dithering & retro
about: Pixel art, dithering, limited palettes and retro CRT looks, in 2D and in 3D rendered at low resolution. This section covers pixel-perfect cameras, palette swaps, dither patterns and the shader tricks that give 3D scenes a PS1 or pixel-art feel.

name: Painterly, sketch & watercolor
about: Watercolour, sketch, oil paint and other hand-made looks in real time. These guides use filters, textures and custom lighting to make scenes look painted or drawn instead of rendered. They tend to be more experimental and more art-led than other shader topics.

name: Water, waves & ripples
about: Water combines waves, foam, depth colour, reflection, refraction and interaction in one effect. This section covers stylised and realistic water shaders, ripples, buoyancy and underwater looks. Start with a simple scrolling-normal shader, then add depth and foam.

name: Sky, clouds & weather
about: Skies, clouds, day-night cycles, rain, snow and fog set the atmosphere of an outdoor scene. These guides cover procedural skyboxes, stylised and volumetric clouds, weather systems and wetness effects. Several of them show how to keep the cost low on mobile.

name: Grass, trees & foliage
about: Grass, trees and foliage need to look dense while staying cheap. This section covers GPU instancing, wind animation, billboards, interactive grass, LODs and stylised leaf shading. Read it before you scatter ten thousand blades of grass.

name: Terrain & landscapes
about: Landscapes in Unity range from the built-in Terrain system to fully procedural meshes. These guides cover terrain painting and layers, heightmaps, splat blending, large-world streaming and custom terrain shaders. Related generation techniques live under Procedural generation.

name: Snow, ice, sand & lava
about: Surfaces that react to the player: footprints in snow, accumulating frost, flowing sand and glowing lava. These guides use render textures, height deformation and tessellation to make the ground respond. Fun to build and visually rewarding.

name: Particles & VFX Graph
about: Particles drive fire, smoke, sparks, magic and impacts. This section covers the built-in Particle System and the GPU-based VFX Graph, how to author effects, control them from code and keep overdraw low. A good first stop for anyone making effects.

name: Fire, magic & impacts
about: Fire, spells, explosions and hit effects are where VFX craft shows. These guides break down specific effects step by step, covering flipbook textures, shaders, timing and the small touches that sell an impact. Useful for learning by recreating.

name: Dissolve, holograms & sci-fi FX
about: Dissolves, holograms, glitches, force fields and other sci-fi effects mostly come from a handful of shader ideas: noise thresholds, fresnel and scanlines. These guides show how to build them and how to animate them from gameplay code.

name: Procedural generation
about: Procedural generation builds content with algorithms: dungeons, terrain, mazes, cities and levels. This section covers noise, cellular automata, wave function collapse, Voronoi maps, hex and grid worlds, and how to keep generated content playable. Good for replayability and for shipping big worlds with a small team.

name: Noise & procedural textures
about: Noise functions are the raw material of much procedural content: terrain, clouds, textures and organic motion. These guides explain Perlin, simplex, Worley and fractal noise, how to combine and animate them, and how to generate them on the GPU.

name: Raymarching & SDF
about: Raymarching with signed distance fields renders shapes from maths alone, with soft shadows, blends and fractals for almost free. These guides cover SDF primitives, operators, lighting and how to use raymarching inside Unity shaders. It is mind-bending the first time and very powerful afterwards.

name: Math for game devs
about: Vectors, matrices, quaternions, curves, easing and interpolation sit under almost everything in games. These guides explain the maths in an intuitive way, with visual examples and Unity code. Worth a read even if you have been shipping for years.

name: Gameplay systems & mechanics
about: Inventories, abilities, quests, dialogue, input, saving and character controllers: the systems that make a game play. This section covers how to design and build them in Unity so they stay flexible as the game grows. Good for getting from prototype to game.

name: Animation, rigging & IK
about: Character and object animation covers the Animator, state machines, blend trees, Animation Rigging, inverse kinematics and procedural animation. These guides show how to make movement feel good and how to drive it from code. Start with state machines, then move to procedural techniques.

name: Physics & collisions
about: Rigidbodies, colliders, joints, raycasts and custom movement define how things collide and feel. This section covers Unity physics in practice, from character controllers to ragdolls, vehicles and destruction, and how to avoid the classic jitter and tunnelling problems.

name: AI, pathfinding & boids
about: Enemies and NPCs need to move and decide. These guides cover NavMesh, A* on grids and graphs, flow fields, steering and boids, behaviour trees and state machines. Pick the method that fits your world: navmesh for 3D levels, grids for tactical and tile games.

name: Cameras & cutscenes
about: Cameras shape how a game is seen: Cinemachine, follow cameras, screen shake, cutscenes with Timeline and split screen. This section shows how to build smooth, flexible camera setups and cinematics without fighting the system.

name: UI & UI Toolkit
about: Interfaces in Unity use uGUI or the newer UI Toolkit. These guides cover layout, scaling, menus, HUDs, animation, performance and building UI that works across screen sizes. Useful before your menus turn into a tangle.

name: Audio
about: Sound is half of how a game feels. This section covers the Audio Mixer, spatial sound, adaptive music, dialogue sounds and middleware such as FMOD and Wwise. Small touches like footsteps and UI sounds are covered here too.

name: Multiplayer & netcode
about: Networked games bring new problems: authority, latency, prediction and synchronisation. These guides cover Netcode for GameObjects, Unity Gaming Services, relay and lobby, and other frameworks. Read the architecture pieces first, because multiplayer is hard to bolt on later.

name: C# & architecture
about: Clean, flexible code keeps a project moving as it grows. This section covers design patterns, dependency injection, events, ScriptableObject architecture, state machines and async code in Unity. Aimed at developers who already have a prototype and feel it getting messy.

name: Performance & optimization
about: Frame rate, memory and load times decide whether a game ships. These guides cover profiling, garbage collection, batching, draw calls, LODs, object pooling and mobile limits. The first lesson is always the same: measure before you optimise.

name: DOTS, ECS, Jobs & Burst
about: DOTS, ECS, the Job System and Burst compile trade flexibility for raw speed, handling huge numbers of entities. This section covers Entities, systems, jobs, Burst, and how to mix them with regular GameObjects. It has a learning curve, but pays off for simulations and crowds.

name: Addressables, assets & loading
about: How content gets into memory matters for load times and build size. These guides cover Addressables, asset bundles, scene loading, streaming and memory management. Useful once your game is large enough to need more than the Resources folder.

name: Data, saving & localization
about: Where game data lives: ScriptableObjects, JSON, save files, config tables and localisation. This section shows how to structure data so designers can edit it and the game can save and load it safely.

name: Editor tools & extensions
about: Custom inspectors, editor windows, gizmos, property drawers and automation make a team faster. These guides show how to extend the Unity Editor, from small helpers to full tools. A great investment on any project longer than a game jam.

name: Debugging & testing
about: Finding and preventing bugs: debug drawing, the Profiler and Frame Debugger, logging, unit tests, play mode tests and automated checks. These guides help you track down problems faster and catch regressions before players do.

name: Builds, version control & DevOps
about: Building, versioning and shipping: Git and LFS, CI pipelines, build automation, platform builds and release workflows. This section covers keeping a Unity project healthy in version control and getting builds out reliably.

name: Libraries, packages & assets
about: Open-source packages and assets that save time, such as UniTask, DOTween, VContainer and many more. These guides introduce what each one does and when it is worth adding. The Repos tab lists them with health checks.

name: 2D games
about: 2D games in Unity cover sprites, tilemaps, 2D lighting, physics and animation. This section includes pixel-perfect setups, platformer and top-down controllers and the 2D renderer. A good starting point for smaller scoped projects.

name: AR & VR
about: AR and VR development covers XR Interaction Toolkit, hand tracking, passthrough and the performance limits of headsets. These guides show how to build comfortable, responsive experiences on Quest, Apple Vision Pro and other devices.

name: Mobile
about: Mobile games need careful handling of performance, battery, screen sizes and store requirements. This section covers optimisation for phones, touch input, safe areas, build size and platform quirks on Android and iOS.

name: Game art breakdowns
about: Breakdowns of how well-known games achieve their looks, from VFX to materials and lighting. They are written for learning by dissecting existing work, and are a source of ideas you can recreate in Unity.

name: Tech art & DCC workflow
about: Technical art sits between art and code: DCC tools, import pipelines, Houdini, Blender, texture workflows and rigging. This section covers getting content into Unity cleanly and building pipelines artists can use.

name: Game design & analysis
about: Design and analysis of why games work: mechanics, level design, pacing, difficulty and player psychology. Not Unity-specific, but useful for turning technical skills into a game people want to play.

name: Courses, series & lectures
about: Longer structured material: full courses, multi-part series and conference lectures. These are good when you want a guided path through a subject instead of single tutorials.
